Firstly, the level range of key influencing factors in the preparation process of GA-FA-CSLNs was determined via single-factor experiments (Additional file 1: Table S2).
On this basis, the Box-Behnken design was employed to systematically optimize the preparation process of these nanoparticles (Additional file 1: Tables S3, S4, Fig.
The final optimized preparation parameters were as follows: glycerol monostearate dosage of 7.697 mg, ultrasonic time of 23.137 minutes, and a mass ratio of Pluronic F-68 to Lipoid E PC S of 3.963:1.

According to the prediction of the optimized model, the response value (Y value) was 73.9, while the actual Y value in the verification experiment was 73.02 ± 1.53 with a relative deviation of <3% (Additional file 1: Table S5), indicating that the optimized process had good reliability and repeatability.
A Malvern particle size analyzer was used to characterize the particle size and zeta potential of GA-FA-CSLNs.
The results showed that the average particle size was 95.5 ± 0.007 nm and the PDI was 0.244 ± 0.012 (Table 1), suggesting a moderate nanoparticle size distribution of the nanoparticles.

Transmission electron microscopy images revealed that GA-FA-CSLNs had a regular spherical shape and uniform dispersion (Figure 1A and B), and the particle size distribution curve exhibited a unimodal pattern (Figure 1C), further confirming the uniform particle size distribution.
The EE% and DL% of each formulation were analyzed using HPLC.
The results showed that all formulations had an EE% of >94% and a DL% of >0.5% (Table 1), indicating that the preparation process had high drug encapsulation capacity and loading efficiency.

The results of the short-term stability experiment (Additional file 1: Table S6) showed that, except for the GA-CSLNs group, no significant changes in particle size and PDI were observed in other formulations after storage at 4 °C for 14 days, suggesting that these formulations had good short-term storage stability.

CSLNs, GA-CSLNs, FA-CSLNs, and GA-FA-CSLNs were prepared by emulsification and sonication.
The glycerol monostearate (8 mg), Lipoid E PC S (70 mg), and CTD (2 mg) were weighed and dissolved in 5 mL of methanol to form the organic phase.
For GA-CSLNs, FA-CSLNs, and GA-FA-CSLNs, 5 mg GA, 5 mg FA, and a mixture of 5 mg GA + 5 mg FA were separately added to the organic phase, respectively.
Pluronic F-68 (280 mg) was weighed and dissolved in 15 mL of water to form the aqueous phase.
The water bath was heated to 55 °C, and the organic phase was slowly injected into the aqueous phase under magnetic stirring (1000 rpm).

The mixture was then stirred at a constant temperature of 55 °C for 1 hour and placed in an ultrasonic cell crusher (SCIENTZ-IID, Ningbo Scientz Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China) for 23 minutes.
The sample was cooled and cured at room temperature, diluted to 20 mL, and then passed through a 0.22 µm microporous filter membrane to obtain CSLN or GA-CSLNs, FA-CSLNs, and GA-FA-CSLNs.

In mainstream clinical practice, HCC is primarily managed via surgical resection, liver transplantation, locoregional therapies, and systemic treatments including tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
However, over 80% of patients are unfortunately diagnosed at an advanced stage, rendering them ineligible for curative interventions such as surgical resection or liver transplantation (Vogl et al.
A tumor-bearing mouse model was constructed by injecting 0.1 mL of a Huh-7 cell suspension (1 × 107 cells/mL) into the axillary region of BALB/c nude mice.

Upon reaching a tumor volume of 64 mm3, 28 nude mice were randomly divided into seven groups: the blank control group, CTD group, CSLNs group, GA-CSLNs group, FA-CSLNs group, GA-FA-CSLNs group, and positive control group.

The control group was administered an equal amount of saline via the tail vein, the positive control group was administered sorafenib (30 µg/10 g) by gavage, and the remaining experimental groups were injected with CTD, CSLNs, GA-CSLNs, FA-CSLNs, or GA-FA-CSLNs (CTD: 3.75 µg/10 g) via the tail vein.
The drug was administered once every two days for a total of seven times.
The long and short diameters of the tumors, the body weights of tumor-bearing nude mice, and their survival status were recorded for each treatment.
On day 15, blood was collected from the retroorbital venous plexus under anesthesia, and the mice were subsequently euthanized via an intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg).
Death was confirmed by the absence of spontaneous breathing, cessation of heartbeat, and loss of corneal reflex, with a waiting period of 5 minutes to ensure irreversible death.
The hearts, livers, spleens, lungs, and kidneys were collected, and the tumors were removed.
The organs and tumors were rinsed in saline, wiped dry, and weighed.
The organs and tumors preserved in 4% paraformaldehyde solution were dehydrated, embedded in paraffin, and sliced with a microtome.

Paraffin sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) to observe the histopathological changes in each group under a microscope and detected via the proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) assay and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) assay to examine the proliferation and apoptosis of the cells.
Standard kits were used to detect liver function indices, including AST and ALT, and kidney function indices, including BUN and Cr.

Body weight monitoring results showed that during the treatment cycle, except for the positive drug sorafenib group, where nude mice showed a significant weight loss, no significant changes in body weight were observed in the nude mice of other experimental groups (Figure 5A).

Survival curve results (Figure 5B) showed that after 14 days of treatment, the survival rates of nude mice in the CSLNs group and GA-CSLNs group were 83.33%, and the survival rate of the GA-FA-CSLNs group reached 100%, while the survival rate of the positive drug group was only 66.67%.
This indicated that GA-FA-CSLNs could significantly prolong the survival time of nude mice, with a better effect than the single-ligand modified groups and the positive drug group.
After 14 days of treatment, the serum biochemical indicators of nude mice were detected.

The results showed that the serum Cr level in the free CTD group was significantly increased (Figure 5C), and the AST and BUN levels in the CSLNs group and positive drug group showed significant abnormalities.

However, all serum biochemical indicators of the GA-CSLNs group, FA-CSLNs group, and GA-FA-CSLNs group were within the normal range, and no obvious liver or kidney function damage was observed, suggesting that GA and FA ligand modification could significantly reduce the hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity of CTD.

As a potent cytotoxic agent, CTD inhibits cancer cell growth and proliferation by inducing DNA damage and triggering apoptosis in a broad spectrum of tumor cells via the extrinsic and intrinsic apoptotic pathways (Naz et al.
CTD significantly inhibited HCC growth and induced endogenous apoptosis by targeting EphB4 to inhibit the downstream JAK2/STAT3 and PI3K/Akt pathways.

However, the clinical application of CTD is limited by its poor water solubility, which poses challenges for formulation development and bioavailability, in addition to its inherent toxicities, including nephrotoxicity, dysphagia, and hepatic congestion (Bischoff 2024).
After confirming the in vitro tumor targeting ability of GA-FA-CSLNs, the CCK-8 assay was used to initially evaluate the in vitro toxicity of each formulation against Huh-7 hepatoma cells.
When Huh-7 cells were co-incubated with different formulations at various drug concentrations for 48 hours, cell viability decreased in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3A).

Compared with the free CTD group, the GA-FA-CSLNs group exhibited the most significant inhibitory effect on Huh-7 cells, with a significantly reduced IC50 (Figure 3B), suggesting that GA-FA-CSLNs had the strongest in vitro toxicity against Huh-7 cells.
The results showed that all formulations could induce apoptosis of Huh-7 cells after 48 hours of intervention, and most apoptotic cells were in the late apoptotic stage.
To deeply explore the molecular mechanism of apoptosis induced by the nanoformulations, Western blotting was used to detect the expression levels of apoptosis-related proteins.

The results (Figure 3E−H) showed that compared with the control group, the expression levels of pro-apoptotic proteins (caspase 3, Bax) in all experimental groups were significantly upregulated (P < 0.01), while the expression level of the anti-apoptotic protein (Bcl-2) was significantly downregulated (P < 0.01).
Among them, the GA-FA-CSLNs group showed the maximum upregulation of caspase 3 and Bax expressions and the maximum downregulation of Bcl-2 expression.
This result was consistent with the flow cytometry results, indicating that GA-FA-CSLNs had the strongest pro-apoptotic effect.

The finally obtained GA-FA-CSLNs had a particle size range of 95–125 nm, and the PDI of all formulations was <0.25, indicating a narrow particle size distribution and good uniformity, which successfully solved the problem of uneven particle size distribution of GA-FA-CSLNs in previous studies.
Particle size is a critical characteristic of lipid-based nanocarriers, as it influences stability, encapsulation efficiency, drug release profiles, and biodistribution.

The vasculature of solid tumors exhibits distinct structural abnormalities compared with normal tissues, including larger and more irregular vessel diameters, increased vessel density, enhanced permeability, and pronounced leakage (Krishnaswami et al.

The leaky tumor vasculature allows circulating nanocarriers with a size below approximately 150 nm to extravasate through the tumor vessel wall and accumulate within the tumor interstitium, thereby increasing the local concentration of chemotherapeutic agents (Han et al.

Therefore, the small particle size and uniform distribution of GA-FA-CSLNs (95.5 nm, PDI < 0.25) are conducive to exploiting the EPR effect, facilitating their penetration across the tumor vascular wall and accumulation in tumor tissue, thus establishing a foundation for subsequent targeted drug delivery (Alfaifi et al.
The surface charge of nanocarriers, typically represented by the zeta potential, is a key determinant of their long-term storage stability.

It is generally accepted that a zeta potential greater than ±30 mV provides sufficient electrostatic repulsion to prevent particle aggregation and maintain colloidal stability (Jain and Thareja 2019).
In the present study, the zeta potential of GA-FA-CSLNs was below ±30 mV, indicating that electrostatic stabilization alone may be insufficient to maintain long-term storage stability.

Notably, the change in zeta potential from −1.26 ± 0.127 mV in unmodified CSLNs to −4.11 ± 0.035 mV in the dual-ligand modified formulation served as indirect evidence of successful surface modification.
